name: Zinc

lead: Zinc is an essential mineral taken as an oral supplement and used in topical products such as zinc oxide sunscreens and acne formulations. People use it for inflammatory acne, redness and hair shedding linked to deficiency.

It supports enzyme function, wound healing, immune regulation and skin-cell biology and has mild anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis found people with acne had lower serum zinc than controls and that zinc treatment, alone or as an adjunct, was associated with significant improvement in inflammatory papule counts, without a significant difference in side effects versus comparators. Benefits are clearest when a deficiency is corrected.

paras: People take it as a daily supplement, often with meals, or use it topically in creams and sunscreens, usually alongside other acne or hair routines. Some pair it with copper because of mineral balance. Skin changes are typically judged over weeks to months.

High-dose supplementation can cause nausea and, over time, copper deficiency, and excess intake may cause ataxia and lethargy. Intake above requirements has not been shown to add benefit. Zinc is available without prescription.

chain: Mineral supports skin and immune function
angle.text: Users take or apply zinc for inflammatory acne, redness and hair shedding tied to deficiency. The mineral supports skin and immune function, so inflammation and shedding ease and skin and hair look healthier. Evidence exists for acne and deficiency-related hair loss; hormone, voice and height claims are anecdotal.

lead: Zinc is an essential trace element in humans, a cofactor for many enzymes and the second most abundant trace metal in the body after iron [1][2]. For appearance it matters in three ways: as an oral supplement and nutrient involved in skin, hair and wound healing; as a topical ingredient, from zinc oxide in sunscreens, barrier creams and mineral makeup to zinc pyrithione in anti-dandruff shampoos; and as a mineral that looksmaxxing forums discuss alongside other supplements [3][4][5][6].

The chain people describe runs from adequate zinc status to calmer inflammatory acne, less shedding where hair loss is tied to deficiency, and better skin repair. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis found that people with acne had lower serum zinc than controls and that zinc treatment, as monotherapy or adjunct, was associated with a significant improvement in inflammatory papule counts, without a significant difference in side effects versus comparators [3]. Wikipedia describes acne, eczema, dry scaling skin, seborrheic dermatitis, impaired wound healing and thin, sparse hair among the signs of zinc deficiency [4].

Wikipedia states that deficiency affects roughly two billion people, mostly in the developing world, and that excess zinc may cause ataxia, lethargy and copper deficiency [1][4]. On looksmax.org zinc is discussed as a routine supplement, often next to peptides such as GHK-Cu, and in threads about forms, amounts and effects on the voice and libido [7][8][9].

paras: Zinc is used orally and topically for inflammatory acne, with proposed anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects [3]. A 2024 review of zinc, copper and iron in selected skin diseases discusses the minerals' roles in skin conditions [10]. Zinc oxide is a skin-protectant ingredient; a US drug label for a zinc oxide diaper cream lists indications to help prevent and treat diaper rash and to protect chafed skin, with warnings for external use only and to avoid contact with eyes [11]. Hair shedding associated with zinc deficiency is described in clinical discussion of the mineral, with benefit generally expected when a deficiency exists [10][12].

Topically, zinc oxide absorbs both UVA and UVB light and is the broadest-spectrum UV absorber the US FDA approves for sunscreens; Wikipedia describes it as photostable and generally considered non-irritating and non-comedogenic, and many sunscreens use nanoparticle forms so that they do not leave a white cast [5]. It is also a main ingredient of mineral makeup, where it appears as CI 77947, and of baby powder, calamine lotion and barrier creams, and athletes use zinc oxide tape [5].

Zinc pyrithione, a zinc coordination compound first described in the 1930s, is the active ingredient in several anti-dandruff shampoos and body washes and is approved for over-the-counter use against dandruff and seborrhoeic dermatitis in the US; it inhibits fungal and bacterial growth [6]. The EU banned its use in cosmetic products from 2021 after classifying it as a category 1B reproductive toxicant, while US rules allow limited concentrations in rinse-off and leave-on products [6].

A 2024 systematic review of 38 randomised trials, commissioned by the WHO for revision of its guidelines, examined zinc for acute and persistent diarrhoea in children [13]. Zinc has also been studied for pneumonia in children, immune function, pressure ulcers, oral mucositis and other conditions [14][15][16][17].

Wikipedia lists acne, eczema, dry scaling skin, seborrheic dermatitis, delayed wound healing and alopecia with thin, sparse hair among the signs of zinc deficiency, together with delayed growth in children [4]. Causes include diets high in phytate-containing whole grains or low in zinc, gut diseases that impair absorption, heavy alcohol use, diarrhoea, chronic kidney or liver disease and bariatric surgery [4]. Mild deficiency from low dietary intake is described as common and severe deficiency as rare [4].

Plasma zinc is described as a limited biomarker; a blood level below about 70 mcg/dL is the usual threshold used with clinical suspicion [4]. Clinicians treat deficiency with oral zinc salts such as gluconate, sulfate or acetate, and the article notes it is unclear whether one form is better [4]. This is the setting in which proponents say zinc visibly changes skin and hair, since the repletion corrects the underlying shortfall.

Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive disorder of zinc absorption caused by variants in the SLC39A4 gene, which encodes a zinc-uptake transporter [18]. It presents, often around weaning, with dermatitis around the body openings and on the fingers and toes, blistering, pustules, diarrhoea and hair loss that can include eyebrows and eyelashes; lifelong zinc supplementation is the treatment [18]. It is the textbook example of a skin and hair condition reversed by zinc [4][18].

Oral zinc has been studied in acne since at least 1978, when a controlled trial of zinc sulfate in acne vulgaris was published [19]. The 2020 meta-analysis reports lower serum zinc in acne patients and better inflammatory papule counts with zinc, and concludes that zinc has been used as monotherapy or adjunct [3]. A 2024 review of zinc, copper and iron in skin disease notes that most cited studies report lower serum zinc in acne patients, while findings on whether levels track severity conflict: some studies linked lower zinc to more severe acne and others found no link [10].

Proposed mechanisms are anti-inflammatory and antibacterial actions and effects on keratinocyte function [3][12]. Researchers also note that zinc status is discussed alongside copper and iron in other skin diseases such as atopic dermatitis and psoriasis, where results on serum levels are inconsistent [10].

Acne: the 2020 meta-analysis reported significantly lower serum zinc in acne patients and an improvement in inflammatory papule counts with zinc treatment, with no significant difference in side-effect incidence [3]. An early controlled trial of zinc sulfate in acne vulgaris was published in 1978 [19].

Other areas: a Cochrane review of nutritional interventions for pressure ulcers (2024) is among the wound-related syntheses [15]; a randomised trial tested zinc chloride mouthwash for chemotherapy-related oral mucositis [16]; and a 2025 randomised trial tested zinc as adjuvant treatment in SARS-CoV-2 [20]. A 2024 crossover trial reported improved absorption of a glycoprotein matrix zinc form [21]. Registered trials include absorption studies of zinc citrate, gluconate and oxide, childhood pneumonia (641 participants) and a large 2026 trial of zinc and infections in older medical patients [22][23][24]. A 2017 review describes zinc as a gatekeeper of immune function [25].

Wikipedia notes that consumption of excess zinc may cause ataxia and lethargy, among other effects [1]. Grokipedia describes zinc as non-toxic at typical dietary levels and notes that inhaling zinc oxide dust can cause metal fume fever [2]. The 2020 acne meta-analysis found no significant difference in side-effect incidence between zinc and comparators [3].

Wikipedia's article on zinc toxicity reports that very high oral intakes can cause nausea, vomiting, cramps and diarrhoea, that long-term high intake has been linked to changes in blood lipids, and that reduced copper levels and zinc-induced sideroblastic anaemia have been described in the literature; the copper changes reversed when zinc intake stopped [26]. Inhaling zinc oxide fumes, for example when welding galvanised steel, can cause metal fume fever [26]. Excess zinc absorption suppressing copper absorption is the reason zinc and copper are often discussed together on forums [1][9][26].

Dietary zinc comes from oysters, red meat, nuts and fortified cereals, per Grokipedia, which gives adult recommended intakes of 11 mg per day for men and 8 mg for women [2]. Wikipedia notes that diets built around high-phytate whole grains, or foods grown in zinc-poor soil, are common causes of low intake [4]. Supplements are sold as sulfate, gluconate, acetate, citrate and oxide salts and as chelated or matrix forms, and registered and published bioavailability trials have compared several of them [27][28][21]. Wikipedia says it is unclear whether any one supplement form is better for treating deficiency [4].

Reviews describe zinc as a cofactor for many enzymes with roles in immune regulation and wound healing, and the acne, wound-healing and dermatitis research builds on those roles [12][25]. Wikipedia adds that zinc is the only metal found in all enzyme classes and is required for prenatal and postnatal development [1].

Zinc is the only metal found in all enzyme classes, is required for prenatal and postnatal development, and deficiency in children is linked to growth retardation, delayed sexual maturation, infection susceptibility and diarrhoea [1]. A 2024 review covers its role in health and disease, including immune regulation and wound healing [12][25]. Absorption differs between forms, which has been compared in small bioavailability trials [21][22].

Zinc ores were used to make brass long before the metal was identified; metallic zinc was produced in India, with distillation evidence at the Zawar mines by the 9th century and the name zincum credited to Paracelsus in the 16th century; Andreas Marggraf is credited with isolating pure zinc in 1746 [1]. Zinc was found in the enzyme carbonic anhydrase in 1940, which showed its biological role, and carboxypeptidase followed in 1955 [1].

Zinc's nutritional status developed in the 20th century: it was found essential for rat growth in 1933 and shown to be essential for human growth in 1963, the first case of acrodermatitis enteropathica was described in 1973, and in 1974 the US National Academy of Sciences declared it essential and set a recommended allowance [4]. The FDA required zinc in total parenteral nutrition fluids from 1978, and the gut zinc transporter ZIP4 was identified in 2002 [4]. In dermatology, zinc sulfate was trialled for acne in 1978 [19], while zinc oxide has an older history as a salve and later as a white pigment and sunscreen ingredient [5].

Zinc is a widely sold dietary supplement, with gluconate, sulfate, acetate, citrate and oxide forms on the market, and bioavailability of different forms has been compared in small trials [27][28][21]. Zinc oxide is regulated in the US as a sunscreen active and skin-protectant ingredient, and is on the FDA's generally-recognised-as-safe list for food use [11][5].

In looksmaxxing communities zinc appears in threads about acne, immunity, and hormonal or voice effects, usually as one item in a supplement stack, and in Turkish-language threads about whether zinc affects erections [29]. Forum members ask which form is best, how long to take it and whether copper should be supplemented afterwards, and answers are anecdotal [7][9].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org zinc is discussed as a routine supplement, often taken with peptides such as GHK-Cu, with threads on amounts, forms, voice effects, libido and what to do after taking too much [7][8][9].

timeline.event: Distillation of nearly pure zinc is evidenced at the Zawar mines in Rajasthan, India [1].
Andreas Marggraf is credited with isolating pure metallic zinc [1].
Zinc is found in carbonic anhydrase, showing its biological importance [1].
Zinc is shown to be essential for human growth [4].
First case of acrodermatitis enteropathica described [4].
US National Academy of Sciences declares zinc essential and sets an allowance [4].
Controlled trial of zinc sulfate in acne vulgaris is published [19].
ZIP4 identified as the gut zinc absorption mechanism [4].
Meta-analysis reports lower serum zinc in acne and improved inflammatory papule counts with zinc [3].
EU bans zinc pyrithione in cosmetic products [6].
